title: Solar food dryer
summary: A black, glazed collector heats air that rises through a shaded cabinet of mesh trays, drying fruit, vegetables, herbs and meat in 1–3 days at 45–60 °C. Built from plywood, a glass or plastic pane, black sheet metal and food-safe mesh. Keeping insects and moisture out matters as much as heat.

materials.item: Glazing: glass pane (fridge shelf, window) or clear plastic sheet, about 0.5–1 m²
Absorber: sheet metal painted matt black
Plywood or boards for the collector box and cabinet
Food-safe mesh for trays: nylon or fibreglass fly screen, or stainless racks
Fine fly screen for every vent
12V fan with a small solar panel, to speed drying
Small solar panel (5–10W) for the fan

steps.text: Choose a site in full sun from mid-morning to late afternoon, with some breeze, off the ground and away from animals.

Build the collector: a shallow box (about 0.6–1 m wide, 1.5–2 m long, 10 cm deep) with black-painted metal on the bottom, insulation under it, and glazing on top. Leave the low end open behind fly screen as the air inlet.
steps.warn: Glass edges cut. Handle panes with gloves and set them in a frame, not loose.

steps.text: Build the cabinet: an upright box with runners for 3–6 trays spaced 8–10 cm apart, a door at the back, and screened vents at the top. Make the cabinet walls solid so sun doesn't hit the food.
Join the collector's top end to the bottom of the cabinet, sloping the collector up towards it at 30–45° and facing the equator. Seal the joint so air can only enter through the inlet.
Make trays: timber frames with food-safe mesh. Don't use galvanised, copper or painted mesh; zinc, copper and old paint leach into acidic food.
Screen every opening with fine fly screen. Insects ruin dried food.
Test empty on a sunny day: tray temperature should reach 45–60 °C around midday. Too hot: open the top vents more. Too cool: close them a little, or improve sealing and glazing.
steps.warn: The absorber and glazing get hot enough to burn. Touch with care.

steps.text: Optional: fit a 12V fan in the top vent, powered straight from a small solar panel. It speeds up when the sun is strong, just when you need more airflow. Red fan wire to the panel's +. A 5–10W panel needs no fuse for a single small fan; add one (1A) if you run it from a battery instead.
Prepare food: slice 3–6 mm thick, evenly. Dip fruit in lemon juice or diluted vinegar to slow browning; blanch most vegetables for 2–4 minutes. Heat meat strips to 71 °C before drying (notes).
Load one layer per tray, not touching. Dry for 1–3 days. Close the vents or bring trays in at night so dew doesn't re-wet the food.
steps.warn: Discard any batch that grows mould, smells off or stays sticky. Mouldy dried food can make you seriously ill.

steps.text: Test dryness: fruit leathery with no moisture when squeezed, vegetables brittle, jerky bends and cracks without snapping. Cool, pack in sealed jars or bags, and store dark and dry. Check jars after a week for condensation.

notes:
## How it works
The collector turns sunlight into warm air, which rises (or is pushed by a fan) up through the trays and out of the top. Warm air holds more water, so it pulls moisture out of the food and carries it away. Shading the food in a cabinet keeps colour and vitamins better than drying in direct sun.

## Sizing
Rough rule: 1 m² of collector for every 1 m² of tray area. Each square metre of collector in good sun puts about 300–500W into the air. Removing 1 kg of water takes roughly 0.7kWh, so 1 m² of collector dries 2–5 kg of fresh fruit (which is 75–90% water) in a sunny day or two.

## Temperatures
| Food | Target |
|---|---|
| Herbs | 35–45 °C |
| Fruit | 50–60 °C |
| Vegetables | 50–60 °C |
| Meat (after pre-heating) | 60–70 °C |

Below about 40 °C food dries slowly and can spoil. Above about 70 °C the outside hardens and traps moisture inside.

## Meat safety
Drying alone may not kill germs in meat. Heat strips to 71 °C (steam or simmer briefly, or bake) before drying. Use lean meat, trim fat (fat goes rancid), and dry until it cracks when bent. This follows widely published food-safety guidance on home jerky.

## Moisture is the enemy
- Bring trays in or close the vents at night.
- Store in airtight containers, in the dark, cool and dry. Add a packet of dry rice or silica gel.
- If condensation appears in a jar within a week, the food isn't dry enough; dry it more.

## If you lack a part
- No glazing: a black-painted collector without glass still warms air by 5–15 °C; drying is slower.
- No mesh: thin sticks or bamboo slats spaced a few millimetres apart, or clean cotton cloth stretched on a frame.
- No collector at all: hang thin strips in a shaded, airy, insect-screened space in hot dry weather.
